claims.text: The initial material is a multiphase eutectic high-entropy alloy containing distinct phases such as an FCC matrix and sigma-phase intermetallics.
A nominally protective oxide film is present on the alloy at elevated temperature.
Sliding contact can rupture an oxide film and thereby promote adhesive and abrasive wear.
Potential differences between phases in a multiphase HEA can produce galvanic corrosion.
Galvanic coupling between constituent phases can cause selective anodic dissolution of one phase.
Multiphase interfaces are preferential sites for oxide decohesion under combined mechanical and chemical stress.
Mechanical removal preferentially strips oxide from the more anodic phases.
Oxide rupture exposes fresh phase surfaces that then dissolve preferentially because of local galvanic differences.
Repeated oxide formation, fracture, mechanical removal, and galvanic dissolution create a self-sustaining degradation cycle.
The coupled cycle accelerates net material loss beyond the sum of independently measured wear and corrosion losses.
Under simultaneous high-temperature wear and corrosion, the multiphase eutectic alloy will degrade faster than a comparable single-phase HEA.
Removing corrosive species from the test environment will reduce total degradation relative to simultaneous wear-corrosion exposure.
Both wear loss and corrosion current will be elevated during simultaneous exposure beyond simple addition of the separate responses.
The synergy is most pronounced when the microstructure has a significant interphase galvanic mismatch and mechanically vulnerable oxide films.
The proposed synergistic acceleration is most pronounced from approximately 600 to 850 degrees Celsius.
Outside the stated phase-contrast or temperature boundaries, oxide rupture and galvanic effects diminish.
Increasing temperature can increase selective dissolution in a eutectic HEA.
The relative contributions of oxide disruption and galvanic dissolution depend on alloy composition and test conditions.
A matched multiphase-versus-single-phase tribocorrosion comparison with electrochemical monitoring and post-test microscopy can test the proposed mechanism.
Failure to observe either excess coupled degradation or localized interfacial oxide disruption and galvanic dissolution would falsify the proposed mechanism.
